tagline.text: A beach on Batan's east coast covered in rounded volcanic rock instead of sand

location.label: Location
location.text: San Joaquin, Basco, Batanes, on the east coast of Batan Island

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–1,500 (per person; Basco tricycle or North Batan tour, excluding flights and lodging)

children.text: Valugan Boulder Beach is a long shore of rounded, smooth andesite boulders on the coast about 3 km east of central Basco. These rocks, flung out by the eruptions of Mount Iraya, have been polished by Pacific waves over centuries, so this is a beach for scenery and photos rather than swimming.
Valugan Boulder Beach lies in San Joaquin, about
3 km

from central Basco on the east coast of Batan Island, the main island of Batanes. "Valugan" is said to mean "east" in the Ivatan language, so the name simply means the east beach of Basco. Instead of a sandy beach, it is a long stretch of rounded boulders, from the size of a human head to the size of a child's body, and one trip report puts the beach at about
3 km
long. It is framed by steep cliffs on one side and grassy hills on the other, with Mount Iraya visible in the distance.

These rocks are andesite. Mount Iraya, an active volcano, rises in the north of Batan Island, and trip reports explain that it erupted at around 325 BC and between AD 286 and 505, throwing out rocks that rolled to the shore and were shaped by waves and wind. Sources differ on the dates, so it is safest to treat the exact timing as uncertain. One trip report gives AD 400 for the same story. At the southern end of the beach there are pebbles and small stones instead of big boulders, and the waves are comparatively calmer.

For travelers, this beach is a place to walk, look and take photos. Sunrise, with the sound of waves hitting rocks and the sky turning red, is popular with photographers, and at the entrance there is a concrete viewing deck with benches, stairs down to the beach, a Virgin Mary grotto-style shrine and traditional Ivatan fishing boats called tataya, which add to the scene. On the right side of the beach you can also see small stacks of stones left by visitors. These waters are said to be a sacred fishing ground for Ivatan fishermen, especially those of San Joaquin, with a traditional fishing season called faypatawen running from March to the end of May.

This guide is for travelers staying in Basco who plan to explore North Batan for half a day or more. Valugan is close to Basco Lighthouse, Vayang Rolling Hills and the Dipnaysuhuan Japanese Tunnel, so it almost always appears in tricycle tours. The distance is short, but the rocks are slippery and the waves are hard to predict, so you need the habit of watching your footing and the waves even while taking photos. No admission fee or operating hours are listed in the sources, and it is known as a beach that is open and effectively free, but check the weather and safety conditions locally. Above the beach, roadside grassy areas open toward the sea, so you can enjoy the view without going down to the rock section. On a day with high waves or after rain, choosing to watch from the viewing deck and head back without going down is also a good way to travel.

The heart of Valugan is the rounded boulders that cover the shore in place of sand. They differ in color and size and have been worn smooth by the waves, and with cliffs and grassy hills as a backdrop they create a distinctive landscape.
The coast faces east, so sunrise photos are popular. You can capture the changing sky before dawn together with spray bursting against the rocks. Early in the morning there are few people.
From the far end of the beach you can see Mount Iraya to the north. On a day without clouds, the boulder beach and the active volcano fit in a single frame.
From a small deck with benches you can look down over the whole beach, and stairs lead down to the shore. Check the terrain and waves from above before you go down to stay safe.

blocks.title: Tataya boats and Virgin Mary shrine

children.text: On one side of the beach sit traditional tataya fishing boats and a small shrine to the Virgin Mary. It is a scene that offers a glimpse of Ivatan life at sea and their faith. Please show respect in front of the shrine.
The south is less awkward underfoot and has gentler waves than the boulder-heavy north. Grass meets the beach, so there are stretches that are easier to walk.

blocks.title: A stop on the North Batan route

children.text: Valugan is a regular stop on North Batan tricycle tours along with Basco Lighthouse and Vayang Rolling Hills. Even visiting all three in one go takes only half a day.
This coast has long been used as a fishing ground by fishermen of San Joaquin, and a traditional fishing season called faypatawen is said to run through the end of
March–May
each year. If you come across fishermen at work, ask permission before taking photos and do not touch their boats or nets.

items.title: Sunrise half-day route
items.subtitle: From Valugan to the lighthouse and grasslands

children.text: Take a tricycle from your Basco lodging to Valugan. Agree on a time with your driver the day before so you arrive before sunrise.
Wait for sunrise on the viewing deck, then go down the stairs to the beach to take photos. The rocks may be wet, so be careful with your footing.
Walk slowly to the pebble stretch at the south end of the beach and enjoy the scenery, taking care not to get close to the waves.
Return to your lodging for breakfast.
Continue by tricycle to Vayang Rolling Hills and Basco Lighthouse.
From Valugan to Basco Lighthouse you head back toward town and take a short tricycle ride. Travel time varies with road conditions.
Meet your tricycle driver at your lodging and start the full-day tour.
Look around the viewing deck and beach at Valugan Boulder Beach.
Visit nearby historical sites such as the Dipnaysuhuan Japanese Tunnel.
Return to central Basco for lunch and a rest.
Head to Vayang Rolling Hills and Basco Lighthouse and watch the scenery around sunset.
The Dipnaysuhuan Japanese Tunnel is listed as about
8.3 km
from Valugan (about
20 minutes
by car).
Take a domestic flight from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Basco Airport (BSO). Wikipedia says PAL Express operates the Manila route.
Small turboprop aircraft are used, so cancellations in bad weather are frequent. Leave extra days before your flight home.
Round-trip fares vary greatly by season, and examples of about ₱10,000–20,000 have been reported.
There are reports that the pre-registration procedure for visiting Batanes has changed, so check provincial government announcements before you leave.
Valugan is about
3 km
from central Basco, a short tricycle ride. There is a report that the access road to the beach was improved in 2019.
Some travelers rent a bicycle or motorbike and go on their own. There are slopes and wind, so consider your stamina.
North Batan tricycle tours were listed in 2014–2018 trip reports at about
for two people. Prices may have risen, so agree on the price in advance with your lodging or driver.
It is also common to be introduced to a guide and driver through your lodging.

Wikivoyage describes the best time for Batanes as the dry season of March–June, when winds and waves are relatively calm. In this period flight cancellations and wave risks are lower, making it a good time to visit Valugan. By contrast, July–September brings frequent rain and typhoons, the waves become rough, and even without a typhoon strong winds can close coastal roads.

To see the sunrise, aim for early morning on a clear day. In the winter, when clouds are common, the sun may be hidden and you may not get the view you expect. On days with high waves, do not go down to the beach; enjoy it from the viewing deck.

There is no lodging or restaurant at Valugan itself; you stay at a guesthouse or small hotel in Basco town and visit from there. Wikivoyage advises that Basco is the only place on Batan with banks, so bring plenty of cash. Lodging fills up early in peak season, so book it together with your flight.

Food in Batanes is known to be expensive because many ingredients are imported. Restaurants in Basco serve Ivatan dishes and seafood, and many lodgings will cook dinner for you. Coconut crab (about ₱800–2,000) is a dish that requires a permit, so eat it only at places that have one.
Wear sneakers or trekking shoes with non-slip soles. Wet rocks are very slippery, and slippers are dangerous.
Walk on rocks higher up where waves do not reach, and do not stand with your back to the sea when taking photos. Large, unpredictable waves can surge up.
Do not take rocks or stones from the beach. Removing stones is known to be prohibited.
For sunrise, agree on a time with your tricycle driver the day before and bring a light jacket and a flashlight.
If you use a tripod, set it on firm ground because the rocks are unstable, and carry a cloth to wipe water droplets from your lens.
Winds are often strong, so keep your hat and light belongings from blowing away.
Phone signal is weak, so save maps offline in advance. Bring plenty of cash as well.
A boulder beach can look monotonous, so for photos try layering the foreground rocks, distant Mount Iraya and the sky. Early morning, when there are few people, is the calmest.
The rocks are slippery and the waves are unpredictable, so swimming is not allowed, and there is a risk of being swept away; do not go near the water.
Swimming is not recommended anywhere around Valugan. Plan swimming and water activities at another beach.
If your foot gets caught in a gap between large rocks you can be hurt, so check each step as you walk. For children and elderly people it is safer to watch from the viewing deck.
In typhoon season coastal roads close and waves become very high. Do not visit when weather warnings are issued.
The Virgin Mary shrine and the fishermen's boats are places of faith and livelihood for residents. Do not climb on or touch them.
The boulder beach has no shade and strong wind. At midday protect yourself from the sun and drink plenty of water.
A white lighthouse on Naidi Hills, a short tricycle ride past town. It combines well with Valugan on a North Batan route.
Green rolling hills where you can see cows and carabaos grazing. It is close to Basco Lighthouse, so it fits well on the same route.
A World War II Japanese military site listed as about
8.3 km
from Valugan. If you are interested in history, add it to a half-day route.
A boulder beach called Valugan's twin, on the west coast of Basco. It is fun to compare with Valugan.
